newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Assembly abolishes drive-through mastectomies.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Assembly abolishes drive-through mastectomies.

text.p: California lawmakers on Monday passed a bill to abolish so-called "drive-through mastectomies" by requiring health insurers to provide 48 hours of in-patient coverage to mastectomy patients.

The bill, approved by the state Assembly, on a 53-15 vote, was introduced by Valerie Brown, a Democratic member of California's state Assembly. Brown said increased efforts by managed care companies to save money on patient care made it necessary to set that kind of limit. The bill now advances to the state Senate.
Brown said there was a five-fold increase between 1991 and 1995 in the number of U.S. women who underwent mastectomies on an outpatient basis.
Such statistics have led critics to call the outpatient surgeries "drive-through mastectomies," and cite them as an example of how health maintenance organizations (HMOs) cut corners on patient care.

"By the end of today, 500 American women will tell their husbands or maybe their grandkids that their doctor's appointment didn't go so well -- that they've been diagnosed with breast cancer. This bill is about protecting those women," Brown said in a statement."

The bill also provides for a minimum of 24 hours of in-patient care following a lymph node dissection, a less radical treatment for breast cancer. It also requires coverage for a follow-up visit with a licensed health care professional after either surgical procedure.

The measure had the support of a broad coalition of senior citizen groups, breast cancer survivors and physicians. Opponents of the bill had argued that patients and doctors should decide on the appropriate length of stay on a case-by-case basis.
A similar bill has been introduced in the U.S. Congress by Representative Rosa DeLauro, a Connecticut Democrat.
